subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (1, 5, 3), (2, 4, 0) and (3, −1, −5), and B is the matrix with rows (2, −1, 0), (0, −2, 5) and (1, 2, 0), then find 3A − 4Bᵀ.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 9(iii), book p.41. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split gives a mark to each of the four separate matrices a student has to put on the page — Bᵀ, 3A, 4Bᵀ and the difference — because the transpose is a full mark's worth of work on its own and is where the answer is usually lost. CHECKED ENTRY BY ENTRY, TWICE: the nine entries were first read off the three intermediate matrices, then recomputed straight from the stem as 3aᵢⱼ − 4bⱼᵢ, and the two passes agree: (−5, 15, 5), (10, 20, −8), (9, −23, −15). The transposed-index trap is visible at two positions: Bᵀ in row 1 column 3 is B's entry in row 3 column 1, which is 1, while Bᵀ in row 3 column 1 is B's entry in row 1 column 3, which is 0. Swapping those two would still leave a well-formed 3×3 matrix, so the check has to be positional. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices supplies questions to all three sections of this paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say the order you would work in to find 3A − 4Bᵀ.

steps.label: Write Bᵀ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write Bᵀ before any scaling. Read B down each column and write that column as a row: column 1 of B is (2, 0, 1), so row 1 of Bᵀ is (2, 0, 1).
steps.memory_tip: Column 1 of B becomes row 1 of Bᵀ. Read B downwards, write Bᵀ across.
lines: Bᵀ turns the columns of B into rows.
B is 3×3, so Bᵀ is 3×3 and matches A.
The 5 moves from row 2 to row 3;
the 1 in row 3 of B moves to row 1 of Bᵀ.

recall.must_convey: That Bᵀ is written by turning each column of B into a row, giving rows (2, 0, 1), (−1, −2, 2) and (0, 5, 0).
accept: read B down its columns and write each column as a row
B transpose has rows two zero one, minus one minus two two, zero five zero
columns become rows so the five moves down to the last row
columns ni rows ga marchi B transpose rasukovali
transpose B first because it is a three by three like A

steps.why: The entry in row i column j of Bᵀ is the entry in row j column i of B. Writing Bᵀ out in full, before any scaling, is what keeps the two indices from being swapped.
common_mistakes: Reading Bᵀ off the rows of B instead of its columns.
Reversing the order of the rows of B instead of exchanging rows with columns.

steps.label: Find 3A
steps.margin_note: Second mark. A scalar multiplies every entry, including the negative ones: 3(−1) = −3 and 3(−5) = −15.
steps.memory_tip: A scalar reaches all nine entries, negatives included. Nothing is left unchanged.
lines: 3A multiplies every entry of A by 3.

recall.must_convey: That every entry of A is multiplied by 3, giving rows (3, 15, 9), (6, 12, 0) and (9, −3, −15).
accept: multiply all nine entries of A by three
three A has rows three fifteen nine, six twelve zero, nine minus three minus fifteen
the scalar three reaches every entry including the negatives
A lo prathi entry ni three tho multiply cheyyali
three times A entry by entry

steps.why: Scalar multiplication is defined entry by entry, so 3A is a single pass over the nine numbers. Doing it as its own step keeps the later subtraction to one clean pass.
common_mistakes: Multiplying only the first row or only the diagonal by 3.

steps.label: Find 4Bᵀ
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Multiply every entry of Bᵀ by 4. Scaling first and transposing afterwards gives exactly the same matrix, since (kB)ᵀ = kBᵀ for any scalar k — the reason to work from Bᵀ is simply that it is already written down.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply every entry of Bᵀ by 4. Scaling before or after transposing gives the same matrix, so work from the Bᵀ already on the page.
lines: 4Bᵀ multiplies every entry of Bᵀ by 4.

recall.must_convey: That every entry of Bᵀ is multiplied by 4, giving rows (8, 0, 4), (−4, −8, 8) and (0, 20, 0).
accept: multiply the transpose by four, not the original B
four B transpose has rows eight zero four, minus four minus eight eight, zero twenty zero
scale each of the nine entries of B transpose by four
B transpose lo prathi entry ni four tho multiply cheyyali
four times the transpose entry by entry

steps.why: The question asks for 4Bᵀ, so the scalar acts on the transpose that has already been written. Keeping this as its own step means the final subtraction is between two finished matrices.
common_mistakes: Transposing from memory instead of reading Bᵀ off the page, so the entries land in the wrong positions.
Writing 4(5) as 9 by adding instead of multiplying.

steps.label: Subtract entry by entry
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Subtract position by position, in the order 3A − 4Bᵀ. Watch the double negatives: 6 − (−4) = 10 and 12 − (−8) = 20.

recall.must_convey: That the two scaled matrices are subtracted position by position, giving rows (−5, 15, 5), (10, 20, −8) and (9, −23, −15).
accept: subtract four B transpose from three A entry by entry
the answer has rows minus five fifteen five, ten twenty minus eight, nine minus twenty three minus fifteen
take away the matching entries, and minus a negative becomes plus
corresponding entries subtract cheste final matrix vasthundi
three A minus four B transpose position by position

steps.why: Subtraction acts on each position separately, so the answer keeps the 3×3 order. Recomputing one or two entries straight from the stem as 3aᵢⱼ − 4bⱼᵢ is a fast check that the transpose was written correctly.
common_mistakes: Computing 4Bᵀ − 3A and getting every sign reversed.
